title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Karenins, husband and wife, went on living in the same house, met every day, and remained complete strangers to each other. Alexey Alexandrovitch made a rule of seeing his wife each day so that the servants would have no grounds for suspicion, but he avoided dining at home. Vronsky never came to Alexey Alexandrovitch's house, but Anna saw him elsewhere, and her husband knew it.

The position was wretched for all three of them, and not one of them could have endured it for a single day if they hadn't expected it to change — if they hadn't believed it was only a temporary, painful ordeal that would pass. Alexey Alexandrovitch hoped that this passion would pass, the way everything passes, that everyone would forget about it, and that his name would remain unblemished. Anna, on whom the situation depended and for whom it was more miserable than for anyone, endured it because she not only hoped but firmly believed that it would all very soon be settled and come out right. She had no idea what would resolve it, but she was sure something would turn up before long. Vronsky, against his own will or wishes, followed her lead, and hoped too that something — apart from anything he himself did — would surely sort it all out.

In the middle of winter Vronsky spent a tedious week. A foreign prince had come to Petersburg on a visit and had been placed in his charge, with Vronsky responsible for showing him the sights. Vronsky cut a distinguished figure; he had the knack of behaving with respectful dignity and was used to dealing with such grand personages — which is why he had been given the prince. But he found the duty very tiresome. The prince was anxious not to miss anything that he might be asked about back home — had he seen this in Russia? — and on his own account he was determined to enjoy every Russian amusement to the full. Vronsky had to be his guide in satisfying both impulses. Mornings they spent driving out to see the sights; evenings they spent enjoying the national entertainments. The prince enjoyed health exceptional even by royal standards. Through gymnastics and careful attention to his condition he had brought himself to the point where, in spite of his excesses in pleasure, he looked as fresh as a big, glossy green Dutch cucumber. The prince had traveled a great deal, and counted as one of the chief advantages of modern transport the accessibility of the pleasures of every nation.

He had been in Spain, where he had indulged in serenades and made friends with a Spanish girl who played the mandolin. In Switzerland he had killed chamois. In England he had ridden in a red coat over hedges and shot two hundred pheasants for a bet. In Turkey he had got into a harem; in India he had hunted on the back of an elephant; and now in Russia he wished to taste all the specifically Russian forms of pleasure.

Vronsky, who was effectively his master of ceremonies, took great pains to arrange all the Russian entertainments suggested for the prince by various people. They had race horses and Russian pancakes and bear hunts and three-horse sledges and gypsies and drinking parties with the Russian accompaniment of broken crockery. And the prince fell in with the Russian spirit with astonishing ease, smashed trays of crockery, sat with a gypsy girl on his knee, and seemed to be asking — what more, and does the whole Russian spirit really come down to just this?

In reality, of all the Russian entertainments the prince liked best French actresses, ballet dancers, and white-seal champagne. Vronsky was used to princes, but either because he himself had changed lately, or because he was in too close proximity to this prince, the week felt dreadfully tiresome. The whole week he felt the way a man might feel set to look after a dangerous madman — afraid of the madman, and at the same time, from being constantly with him, afraid for his own sanity. Vronsky was continually aware that he couldn't relax for a second from the tone of stern, official respect, or he himself might be the one insulted. The prince's manner toward the very people who, to Vronsky's surprise, were ready to stoop to any depth to provide him with Russian amusements was contemptuous. His comments on the Russian women he was supposedly there to study made Vronsky flush with indignation more than once. The chief reason the prince was so particularly disagreeable to Vronsky was that he couldn't help seeing himself in him. And what he saw in this mirror did not flatter his self-esteem. Here was a very stupid, very self-satisfied, very healthy, very well-washed man, and nothing more. He was a gentleman — true, and Vronsky couldn't deny it. He was even-tempered and not obsequious with his superiors, free and engaging with his equals, and contemptuously indulgent with his inferiors. Vronsky was the same, and considered it a great merit. But to this prince he was an inferior, and the prince's contemptuously indulgent manner toward him revolted him.
"Brainless beef! Can I really be like that?" he thought.

Be that as it might, when on the seventh day he parted from the prince, who was setting off for Moscow, and received his thanks, he was happy to be rid of his uncomfortable position and the unpleasant reflection of himself. He said goodbye at the station on their return from a bear hunt where they had been treated to a display of Russian prowess that had gone on all night.
